newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Regulatory concerns tarnish Westpac bid.
newsitem.headline: Regulatory concerns tarnish Westpac bid.

text.p: Market enthusiasm for Westpac Banking Corp's A$1.435 billion bid for Bank of Melbourne Ltd waned on Friday due to fears that regulatory and government approval for the friendly deal was not assured.
The two-day share price run by Bank of Melbourne ran out of puff on Friday, with the stock slipping three cents to A$9.47 after rising 70 cents on Thursday and 65 cents on Wednesday.
The Australian Stock Exchange has begun an investigation into the share surge, with an exchange spokesman saying the timing of the merger announcement was under scrutiny.

"There's still a few unknowns here and if you listen to the rhetoric in the papers from the regulator and the politicians, it's not a fait accompli," said one Sydney industry analyst, who asked not to be named.
"What we're seeing here is just a bit of readjustment of expectations," the analyst said.
Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said on Thursday that Westpac's move was a risky one ahead of the release of findings from the Wallis inquiry into Australia's financial system.

The inquiry's report, which was now in the hands of the government and set for public release sometime next week, was expected to support further takovers by the big four banks of their smaller rivals and other finance groups.

Australia's anti-monopolies body, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, said it would have to be convinced of the market benefits arising from the takeover before it would give its blessing.

Westpac has more than A$121 billion of assets while Bank of Melbourne has less than A$10 billion, but analysts said the Sydney-based giant was most attracted to the target's market share in the southern state of Victoria.
Traders and analysts also said Westpac might have underestimated the attrition of Bank of Melbourne customers because of the merger.

"The figures that were given out yesterday show they (Westpac) had six or seven percent spillage (customer loss) from the Challenge acquisition. That was a very stable book. BML is not a stable book." said ANZ Securities analyst Greg Tucker.

Bank of Melbourne has about nine percent of the Victorian market, providing a boost for Westpac which wants to more effectively compete in the affluent market with its major bank rivals National Australia, ANZ, and Commonwealth.
The stock exchange inquiry was not expected to have any bearing on the deal, but could prove interesting anyway, one analyst said.
"There's no effect. It's not easy to get people for insider trading," said one analyst, who asked not to be named.
